+ 'Waite includes the possibility of concord while the parties remain armed, then limits how favourable that harmony should be considered. His entry supports a reading in which tension and cooperation coexist; it does not establish that a disagreement has ended. Our exercise below develops a contemporary distinction between an agreed pause and an assumed peace. That distinction is an editorial application, not a procedure prescribed by Waite. Read Waite’s Two of Swords entry Observe before assigning roles. The blindfold and crossed swords are visible. Both swords are held by one figure: the image does not show two people agreeing to anything. Write one observation, such as “the figure holds a defended position,” separately from an interpretation such as “we are keeping a disagreement contained.” Do not assign one sword to each person as if the picture had established their intentions. Name the source and the lens. Note that Waite allows qualified harmony in an armed state. For this exercise, you may ask whether a pause lets people keep working together while a difference remains. That is one possible use of his entry. The modern hesitation reading elsewhere in this article remains available; neither interpretation proves what a partner feels, promises reconciliation, or guarantees a relationship outcome. Check what makes the pause mutual. Can both people describe what is paused, what may continue, and when they will review it? What fact would end the pause earlier, and what will they do if no agreement emerges? Confirm these conditions in an actual conversation. If only one person knows the plan, treat the agreement as unconfirmed rather than filling the gap with the card. Original hypothetical teaching example, all facts invented. Two volunteers disagree over a poster for a community exhibition: one wants a larger image, the other more explanatory text. For this exercise, they deliberately choose upright Two of Swords for a position asking “How can we work together until we have compared the drafts?” They explicitly agree to pause layout changes for two days while continuing to check captions and image permissions. At Friday’s meeting, they will compare two mockups against agreed needs: can an unfamiliar reader find the event details and read the description on a phone? If they cannot settle the new layout by the deadline, both have already agreed to use the approved existing version for this event. If a factual error appears sooner, they will correct it without reopening every design choice. Here the pause has a shared scope, useful work, a review point and an agreed fallback. These stated facts support the reading; the card supplies none of them. A quiet two days would still not demonstrate that their design preferences had converged. At review, they should record what they actually agreed and any difference that remains. Counterexample: if one volunteer stops replying and the other assumes this means approval, there is no established mutual pause. Ask whether and when the other person is willing to discuss the draft; do not describe silence as consent or draw more cards to determine an absent person’s intention. An unanswered request remains unanswered. For a different emphasis, Four of Swords can help compare rest with the effort of maintaining this balance; Justice asks whether the proposed criteria and responsibilities can be explained fairly. These are comparisons between reading questions, not a rule that one card must replace another. Use the tarot table to practise the three records with a bounded question; record the actual draw separately from this deliberately chosen teaching card.'
